passages.original: Difficile namque ex hoc morbo quisque recipit medicina n, qui non vult patefacere culpam. Rara enim ex hoc confessio, quia sæpe aliud pro alio dicitur, et ideo ad salutem nunquam venitur, de quo ad populum Leatus Cyprianus scripsit. Satis sollicitam ori tuo pone custodiam : nec quisquam facilius quam per linguam peccati coatrahit macutam, teste Jacobo apostolo : Linguam nullus hominum domare potest (Jac. III, 8). Unde pie admonet. diceus : Si quis putat se religiosum esse, non refrenans linguam suam, sed seducens cor suum, hujus vana est religio (Jac. I, 26). Juxta sententiam sapientissimi Salomonis : Qui dimittit aquam, caput est jurgiorum (Prov. XVII, 14); quia qui linguam non refrenat, concordiam dissipat. Unde et Apostolus illum asserit esse perfectum, qui non offenderit in verbo. Sed multi, dum iudiscrete silentium custodiunt, quod prodesse proximis per verbum poterat subtrahunt;
passages.english: For it is hard for anyone to receive a cure for this disease who is unwilling to disclose his fault. Confession of it is rare, because often one thing is said in place of another, and so salvation is never reached; concerning this the blessed Cyprian wrote to the people. Set a careful enough guard on your mouth: no one more easily contracts the stain of sin than through the tongue, as the apostle James testifies: "No human being can tame the tongue" (Jas. 3:8). Hence he admonishes piously, saying: "If anyone thinks himself to be religious, not bridling his tongue but deceiving his heart, this man's religion is vain" (Jas. 1:26). According to the saying of the most wise Solomon: "He who lets out water is the head of quarrels" (Prov. 17:14), because he who does not bridle his tongue scatters concord. Hence the Apostle too declares that man to be perfect who has not offended in word. But many, while they keep silence without discretion, withhold what could have benefited their neighbours through speech;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently: "medicina n" (medicinam), "Leatus" (beatus), "coatrahit macutam" (contrahit maculam), "diceus" (dicens), "iudiscrete" (indiscrete). The attribution to Cyprian is as the text gives it. "The Apostle ... not offended in word" is in fact James 3:2. The sentence continues into the following context.
